events.title: The Dream at Gibeon
events.subtitle: The night God asked, What shall I give you?
story: Smoke rose without end over the great high place at Gibeon. Solomon son of David had not been king for long, and he offered a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. That night, as the flames died down, the young king fell asleep there. In his dream the Lord appeared and spoke: “What would you like me to give you? Ask.”

Solomon answered: “You showed great love to my father David. But I am like a little child; I do not even know how to go out or come in. I have been given charge of a people too many to count, so give me a listening heart, to judge them and to tell good from evil.” He had not asked for a long life, or for riches, or for the lives of his enemies, and his words pleased the Lord.

God said, “Because you have asked for this, I will give you a wise and discerning heart. I will also give you what you did not ask for, riches and honor.” Solomon woke up, and it had been a dream. He went back to Jerusalem, stood before the ark of the covenant to offer sacrifices, and held a feast for all his servants. Later a song bearing Solomon's name would sing it this way: the Lord gives sweet sleep to those he loves.

words.text: What would you like me to give you? Ask.
Give your servant a listening heart, so that I can judge your people and tell good from evil.
Because you did not ask for a long life or riches or the lives of your enemies, but asked for wisdom to discern what is right, I will do as you have asked.
I will also give you what you did not ask for, riches and honor. As long as you live, no king will be your equal.

events.note: Gibeon was a town in the land of Benjamin, about ten kilometers northwest of Jerusalem. Chronicles tells us that before the temple was built, the tent of meeting from Moses' day and the bronze altar stood at the high place here.
events.reflect: If God told me to ask for anything, what would I ask for?

quiz.q: In the dream at Gibeon, what did Solomon ask God for?
options: A listening heart to judge the people
quiz.explain: Solomon asked for a listening heart to judge the people and tell good from evil, and God added the riches and honor he had not asked for (1 Kgs 3:9–13).

events.title: Two Women and One Baby
events.subtitle: A mother's heart revealed before the sword
story: Two women stood before the king. One of them held a living baby in her arms. The woman without a baby spoke first: “My lord, this woman and I live in the same house. We both gave birth to sons, three days apart, and in the night this woman lay on her own child, and he died. Then in the middle of the night, while I was asleep, she took my son and laid the dead child in my arms.”

The woman without a baby went on: “In the morning I got up to nurse my son, and he was dead. But when I looked closely in the daylight, he was not the son I had borne.” The woman holding the baby shouted, “No! The living child is my son, and the dead one is yours.” There was no witness at all. Only the two women's voices clashed in the palace.

King Solomon said, “Bring me a sword. Cut the living child in two and give each woman half.” Then the living child's real mother, her heart aching for her son, cried out, “My lord, give the living child to her, only do not kill him!” The woman who had been holding the baby said, “Divide him, so that he will be neither mine nor yours.” The king pointed to the woman who had begged for the child's life and gave his ruling: “Give the living child to that woman, and do not kill him. She is his mother.”

words.text: Cut the living child in two, and give half to this woman and half to that one.
My lord, give the living child to her. Please, only do not kill him.
Give the living child to that woman, and do not kill him. She is his mother.

events.note: In ancient Israel the king was the highest judge, and anyone who had been wronged could come before him and plead their case. When all Israel heard this ruling, they stood in awe of the king, because they saw that the wisdom of God was in him.
events.reflect: When my own judgment falls short, do I seek God's wisdom first?

quiz.q: What did Solomon have brought in to find the real mother?
quiz.explain: Solomon had a sword brought and ordered the child divided, and the woman who wanted the child to live was shown to be the real mother (1 Kgs 3:24–27).

events.title: The Temple Filled with Cloud
events.subtitle: A house for the one whom heaven cannot hold
story: At the feast in the seventh month, the priests carried the ark of the covenant up from the City of David to the new temple. Inside the ark there was nothing but the two stone tablets Moses had placed there at Horeb. The ark was set in the Most Holy Place under the wings of the two cherubim, and the moment the priests came out, a cloud filled the temple. The glory of the Lord covered the house, and the priests could not even stand to serve.

Solomon stood before the altar in front of the whole assembly, then knelt down, spread out his hands toward heaven and prayed: “Will God really live on the earth? Heaven, even the highest heaven, cannot contain you, so how much less this house I have built! But when your people pray toward this place, hear from heaven and forgive. Even when a foreigner comes from a distant land and prays, hear him too.”

When he had finished praying, the king rose from his knees and blessed the people. Twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep were offered as peace offerings, and the feast went on for seven days and then seven more, fourteen days in all. The people blessed the king and went home to their tents with glad hearts. In later years those who longed for this temple sang: one day in your courts is better than a thousand anywhere else.

words.text: Will God really live on the earth? Heaven, even the highest heaven, cannot contain you, so how much less this house I have built!
When your people pray toward this place, hear from heaven where you live, and when you hear, forgive.
When a foreigner who is not one of your people hears of your name and comes from a distant land and prays toward this house, hear that prayer too.
Praise the Lord, who has given rest to his people just as he promised. Not one of the good promises he made through Moses has fallen to the ground.

events.note: The temple was dedicated in the seventh month, Ethanim, around the Feast of Tabernacles. The Most Holy Place was a cube-shaped room twenty cubits on each side, and only the high priest entered it, once a year.
events.reflect: When I worship, how glad am I to be in God's presence?

quiz.q: When the ark was brought into the Most Holy Place, what was inside it?
quiz.explain: There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets Moses had placed there at Horeb (1 Kgs 8:9).

events.title: The Queen of Sheba's Visit
events.subtitle: Not even half had been told
story: A long line of camels loaded with spices came in through the gates of Jerusalem. Many of the loads held gold and precious stones. It was the queen of Sheba, from a far country in the south. She had heard of Solomon's fame and of the name of the Lord, and she had come a long way to test the king with hard questions. The queen asked him everything that was on her heart.

Solomon answered every question, and nothing was too hard for him. The queen saw the king's wisdom and the palace he had built. She saw the food on his table, his officials seated in rows, the dress of those who served him, his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings the king went up to offer at the house of the Lord. It left the queen breathless.

The queen said to the king, “The report I heard in my own country was true. I did not believe it until I came and saw it with my own eyes, and not even half had been told to me. Praise the Lord your God, who has delighted in you. Because he loves Israel forever, he has made you king to do justice and what is right.” The queen gave Solomon a hundred and twenty talents of gold and spices, and went home to her own land.

words.text: I did not believe what I heard until I came and saw it with my own eyes. And not even half had been told to me.
How blessed are your servants, who stand before you every day and hear your wisdom!
Praise the Lord your God, who has delighted in you. Because he loves Israel forever, he has made you king to do justice and what is right.

events.note: Sheba is thought to have been a kingdom in the southwest of the Arabian Peninsula, in what is now Yemen. It grew rich on the trade in spices such as frankincense and myrrh, and camel caravans traveled north and south along the Red Sea.
events.reflect: Could people see God's goodness through my life?

quiz.q: What did the queen of Sheba say after meeting Solomon?
options: Not even half had been told to her
The wisdom of her own country was greater
quiz.explain: The queen said she had not believed it until she came and saw it, and that not even half had been told to her (1 Kgs 10:7).

events.title: A Heart Turned Away
events.subtitle: The old king's heart turns away
story: A strange altar rose on the hill facing Jerusalem. It was a high place for Chemosh, the god of Moab, and beside it another went up for Molech, the god of the Ammonites. The man who built them was King Solomon, who had once asked for wisdom at Gibeon. His foreign wives burned incense and offered sacrifices there. The smoke climbed into the sky across from the temple.

Besides Pharaoh's daughter, Solomon loved women from Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon and the Hittites. These were the very nations of which the Lord had said, Do not marry them, for they will turn your hearts to other gods. He had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines. As Solomon grew old, his wives turned the king's heart away. The king followed Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Milcom, the god of the Ammonites.

The Lord was angry. He had appeared to Solomon twice. The Lord said to Solomon, “Since you have not kept my covenant, I will surely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant. But for the sake of your father David, I will do it in your son's day. And I will not tear away the whole kingdom; for the sake of David and of Jerusalem, which I have chosen, I will leave one tribe to your son.”

words.text: Since you have not kept my covenant and my commands, I will surely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.
For the sake of your father David, I will not do it while you live; I will tear it out of your son's hand.
I will not tear away the whole kingdom. For the sake of my servant David and of Jerusalem, which I have chosen, I will give one tribe to your son.

events.note: The southern summit of the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem, was later called the Mount of Corruption. The high places Solomon built there stood for some three hundred years, until King Josiah defiled them and tore them down.
events.reflect: What is slowly drawing my heart away from God?

quiz.q: Solomon built a high place on the hill facing Jerusalem for which god of Moab?
quiz.explain: On the hill east of Jerusalem Solomon built high places for Chemosh, the detestable god of Moab, and for Molech of the Ammonites (1 Kgs 11:7).

events.title: Ahijah's Cloak in Twelve Pieces
events.subtitle: The prophet who tore his new cloak
story: Jeroboam, a man of Ephraim, was the son of a widow. When Solomon was building up the city, he saw how hard this young man worked and put him in charge of all the laborers from the house of Joseph. One day, as Jeroboam was leaving Jerusalem, he met the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh on the road. Ahijah was wearing a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the open country.

Suddenly Ahijah took hold of his new cloak and tore it into twelve pieces. Ahijah said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces for yourself. This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: I am going to tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and give you ten tribes. For he has forsaken me and bowed down to other gods. But for the sake of my servant David, I will leave him one tribe.”

Ahijah went on with the Lord's message: “If you walk in my ways as my servant David did, I will be with you and build you a lasting house, as I did for David. I will humble David's descendants, but not forever.” After this Solomon tried to kill Jeroboam. Jeroboam fled to Shishak king of Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died.

words.text: Take ten pieces for yourself. The Lord says he will tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and give ten tribes to you.
I will leave one tribe to his son, so that my servant David may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem.
If you listen to me and walk in my ways as my servant David did, I will be with you and build you a lasting house.

events.note: Ahijah's hometown of Shiloh was where the tent of meeting and the ark of the covenant had stood in the days of the judges. Tearing a garment was a sign-act, a way for a prophet to show God's word before people's eyes, and Samuel had once said something similar to Saul.
events.reflect: Am I clinging to what God entrusted to me as if it were my own?

quiz.q: How many pieces of his cloak did Ahijah give to Jeroboam?
quiz.explain: Ahijah tore his new cloak into twelve pieces and gave ten of them to Jeroboam, announcing that God would give him ten tribes (1 Kgs 11:30–31).

events.title: The Harsh Answer at Shechem
events.subtitle: A cry to lighten the yoke
story: When Solomon died, his son Rehoboam went to Shechem. All Israel had gathered there to make him king. Jeroboam, who had been hiding in Egypt, was sent for and stood before the people too. The people said to Rehoboam, “Your father put a heavy yoke on us. Lighten that hard labor, and we will serve you.” Rehoboam answered, “Come back to me in three days.”

Rehoboam first asked the elders who had served Solomon. The elders advised him, “If today you will be a servant to this people and answer them with kind words, they will be your servants forever.” Rehoboam rejected their advice and asked the young men he had grown up with. The young men said, “Tell them, My little finger is thicker than my father's waist. Tell them, My father beat you with whips, but I will beat you with scorpions.”

On the third day Rehoboam answered harshly, just as the young men had told him. The Lord had turned things this way so that the word he had given Jeroboam through Ahijah of Shiloh would come true. The people cried out, “What share do we have in David? To your tents, Israel!” Adoram, the overseer Rehoboam sent to them, was stoned to death, and the king jumped into his chariot and fled to Jerusalem.

words.text: If today you will be a servant to this people, serve them, and answer them with kind words, they will be your servants forever.
My father made your yoke heavy, but I will make it heavier still. My father beat you with whips, but I will beat you with scorpions.
What share do we have in David? To your tents, Israel! Now look after your own house, David!

events.note: Shechem was the heart of the northern tribes, where Abraham first built an altar and where Joshua renewed the covenant. From that day on, the ten northern tribes were called Israel, and the south was called Judah.
events.reflect: Do I accept the hard truth I need rather than words that are pleasant to hear?

quiz.q: How did Rehoboam decide to answer the people's request?
options: He lightened the yoke, as the elders advised
He handed the kingdom to Jeroboam
He said he would make the yoke heavier, as the young men advised
quiz.explain: Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice and answered harshly, as the young men had said, that he would make the yoke even heavier (1 Kgs 12:13–14).

events.title: The Golden Calves of Bethel and Dan
events.subtitle: To keep them from going to Jerusalem
story: Jeroboam, now the first king of northern Israel, fortified the city of Shechem and lived there. But at night one thought would not let him go. Jeroboam said to himself, “If these people go up to offer sacrifices at the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, their hearts will turn back to Rehoboam king of Judah. Then they will kill me and go back to Rehoboam.”

After taking counsel, the king made two golden calves. Jeroboam said to the people, “Isn't it too hard for you to go all the way up to Jerusalem? Here are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” They were the very words the people had shouted before the golden calf in the wilderness. One calf was set up at Bethel in the south, and the other at Dan in the far north.

This became a sin. The people went in a long procession all the way to Dan to worship one of the calves. Jeroboam built shrines on high places and appointed priests who were not from the tribe of Levi. He copied the feast of Judah and made the fifteenth day of the eighth month a feast day, a month he had chosen on his own. On that day Jeroboam went up to the altar at Bethel and stood there to burn incense.

words.text: If these people go up to offer sacrifices at the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, their hearts will turn back to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me.
It is too hard for you to go up to Jerusalem. Here are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.

events.note: Dan lay at the northern edge of Israel and Bethel near its southern border, so together they blocked the road to Jerusalem from both ends. Bethel was also where Jacob had seen a ladder reaching to heaven.
events.reflect: Am I compromising with God's word to hold on to my position?

quiz.q: In which two places did Jeroboam set up the golden calves?
quiz.explain: Jeroboam set up one golden calf at Bethel and the other at Dan (1 Kgs 12:29).

events.title: The Man of God from Judah
events.subtitle: The man who cried out against the altar
story: Just as Jeroboam was about to burn incense beside the altar at Bethel, a man of God who had come from Judah cried out against the altar: “Altar, altar, this is what the Lord says: A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David, and on you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places and burn human bones. This is the sign: this altar will split apart and its ashes will pour out.”

The king stretched out his hand and shouted, “Seize him!” His hand dried up where it was, and he could not pull it back; the altar split apart and the ashes poured out. The man of God prayed, and the king's hand was restored. The king told him to come home with him, rest, and receive a gift, and the man of God answered, “Even if you gave me half your palace, I would not go with you. The Lord commanded me, Do not eat bread or drink water here, and do not go back the way you came.”

But an old prophet from Bethel came after him and said, “I am a prophet too. An angel told me to bring you home and feed you.” It was a lie. The man of God went back with the old prophet and ate bread, and on the road home a lion killed him. The lion and the donkey stood quietly beside the body. The old prophet took up the body, buried it in his own tomb, and wept, saying, “Oh, my brother!”

words.text: Altar, altar, this is what the Lord says: A son named Josiah will be born to the house of David, and on you he will sacrifice the priests of the high places.
Even if you gave me half your palace, I would not go with you. The Lord commanded me not to eat bread or drink water here.
When I die, bury me in the tomb where the man of God is buried, and lay my bones beside his bones. What he cried out against the altar at Bethel will surely come true.

events.note: This prophecy came true about three hundred years later, when Josiah king of Judah tore down the altar at Bethel and burned the bones from the tombs. Only the tomb of this man of God and the old prophet did Josiah leave untouched.
events.reflect: When words that sound convincing differ from God's word, which do I follow?

quiz.q: Which king from the house of David did the man of God name when he prophesied against the altar at Bethel?
quiz.explain: The man of God cried out that a son named Josiah would be born to the house of David and would sacrifice the priests of the high places on that altar (1 Kgs 13:2).

events.title: The Queen in Disguise
events.subtitle: The blind prophet already knew
story: Jeroboam's son Abijah fell sick. Jeroboam said to his wife, “Disguise yourself so no one will know you are the queen, and go to Shiloh. The prophet Ahijah is there, the one who told me I would be king. He will tell you what will happen to the boy.” The queen took ten loaves, some cakes and a jar of honey, and set out. By then Ahijah was old, and his eyes had grown so dim that he could not see.

The Lord had told Ahijah beforehand, “Jeroboam's wife is coming to ask you about her son, and she will pretend to be another woman.” When Ahijah heard her footsteps at the door, he said, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be someone else? I have been sent to you with heavy news.” The queen in disguise stood frozen where she was.

Ahijah gave her the Lord's message for Jeroboam: “I raised you up from among the people and made you leader over Israel, but you made other gods and idols and threw me behind your back.” Then Ahijah said to the queen, “When your feet enter the city, the boy will die. Of Jeroboam's house, only this boy will be laid in a grave. For in him there is something good toward the Lord.” The queen went back to Tirzah, where the palace was, and as she crossed the threshold the boy died.

words.text: Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be someone else? I have been sent to you with heavy news.
I raised you up from among the people and made you leader over Israel, but you made other gods and idols and threw me behind your back.
Of Jeroboam's house, only this boy will be laid in a grave. For in him there is something good toward the Lord.

events.note: Tirzah was a beautiful town northeast of Shechem, and it was the capital of northern Israel from Jeroboam's time until Omri built Samaria. From Shiloh to Tirzah was probably a little over a day's walk.
events.reflect: Rather than hiding my wrongs, do I admit them before God?

quiz.q: How did Ahijah, whose eyes were dim, recognize the disguised queen?
options: He saw the gifts she brought
A servant whispered it to him
quiz.explain: The Lord told Ahijah beforehand that Jeroboam's wife would come pretending to be another woman (1 Kgs 14:5–6).

events.title: Gold Shields Become Bronze
events.subtitle: The palace shields lose their shine
story: The palace guards lined up before the king, holding their shields. They were not the gold shields that once flashed in the sunlight, but dull bronze ones. Rehoboam son of Solomon became king at forty-one and reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem. His mother was Naamah, an Ammonite woman. In those days Judah set up high places, sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.

In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem. Shishak carried off every treasure of the temple of the Lord and of the palace. The gold shields Solomon had made were all taken too. Solomon's splendor, which had once left the queen of Sheba breathless, was carted off in a foreign king's wagons in less than a generation.

In place of the gold shields Rehoboam made bronze shields and entrusted them to the captain of the guard who kept the palace gate. Whenever the king went into the temple, the guards carried the shields out, and afterward they took them back to the guardroom. There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days. Later, looking at the fallen house of David, a poet sang: Lord, where is your love of old, which you swore to David?

words.text: This is what the Lord says: You have abandoned me, so I have abandoned you into the hand of Shishak.
They have humbled themselves, so I will not destroy them. I will soon rescue them, and I will not pour out my anger on Jerusalem through Shishak's hand.
Lord, where is your love of old, which in your faithfulness you swore to David?

events.note: Shishak is thought to be Shoshenq I of Egypt's Twenty-second Dynasty. A wall of the temple at Karnak is carved with a list of the Canaanite towns he conquered on this campaign. Second Chronicles 12 records that the prophet Shemaiah brought the Lord's word to the king at this time.
events.reflect: Am I dressing up the outside while ignoring the faith I have lost?

quiz.q: After Shishak took the gold shields, what kind of shields did Rehoboam make instead?
quiz.explain: When Shishak took all of Solomon's gold shields, Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place and entrusted them to the captain of the guard (1 Kgs 14:26–27).

events.title: The Rain Will Stop
events.subtitle: One sentence that shut the sky
story: A princess of Sidon came into the palace on the hill of Samaria. Ahab king of northern Israel had married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of Sidon. Ahab built a temple for Baal in Samaria and set up an altar in it. He also made an Asherah pole. Ahab angered the Lord more than any king before him.

Baal was worshiped as the god who held the rain and the storm. People believed that only by praying to Baal would the sky open and grain grow in the fields. One by one, the people of Israel knelt before Baal's altars too. The voices calling on the name of the Lord grew fainter and fainter.

Then Elijah the Tishbite, from Gilead, stood before the king. Elijah said to Ahab, “As surely as the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, whom I serve, there will be neither dew nor rain in the next few years unless I say so.” Now it was the sky's turn to answer who gives the rain. A psalmist sang it this way: you water the mountains from your high places, and the earth is filled with the fruit of your work.

words.text: As surely as the Lord, the God of Israel, lives, whom I serve, there will be neither dew nor rain in the next few years unless I say so.
It is not I who have troubled Israel, but you and your father's house, because you abandoned the Lord's commands and followed the Baals.

events.note: In Canaan and Phoenicia, Baal was worshiped as the god of rain and storm. Elijah's announcement that the rain would stop asked head-on who really gives the rain, Baal or the Lord. Samaria was the new capital of northern Israel, built by Ahab's father Omri.
events.reflect: What do I believe will keep me safe?

quiz.q: Ahab's wife Jezebel was the daughter of the king of which nation?
quiz.explain: Ahab married Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and served Baal (1 Kgs 16:31).

events.title: The Ravens at the Brook Cherith
events.subtitle: A table set by ravens
story: When Elijah left the king, the word of the Lord came to him. The Lord said, “Leave here, go east, and hide by the Brook Cherith, east of the Jordan. Drink from the brook. I have already commanded the ravens to feed you there.” Elijah set out, just as the Lord had said.

Deep in the ravine, a brook trickled between the rocks. When morning came, black wings flapped down. The ravens brought bread and meat. They did the same in the evening. Birds the law called unclean carried the prophet's meals to him. Elijah drank from the brook and lived from one day to the next.

But the sky stayed shut. Day by day the sound of the water grew thinner. The pools shrank, the wet stones dried white, and at last the brook bed lay bare. The drought Elijah had announced had now dried up even Elijah's own stream.

words.text: Leave here, go east, and hide by the Brook Cherith, east of the Jordan.
Drink from the brook. I have already commanded the ravens to feed you there.

events.note: The Brook Cherith is thought to be a ravine on the Gilead side, east of the Jordan, but its exact location is unknown. Many such ravines carry water only in the rainy season, so when drought went on they soon dried up. Ravens were unclean birds the law did not allow people to eat.
events.reflect: Do I remember the small grace God provided for me today?

quiz.q: When did the ravens bring Elijah food?
quiz.explain: The ravens brought Elijah bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook (1 Kgs 17:6).

events.title: The Widow's Jar of Flour at Zarephath
events.subtitle: The last handful of flour
story: The Lord sent Elijah to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, which Jezebel's father ruled. At the town gate a widow was gathering dry sticks. When Elijah asked for water and a piece of bread, the widow said, “All I have is a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. I am going to make one last meal for my son and me, and then we will die.”

Elijah said, “Don't be afraid. First make a small loaf for me and bring it to me, and then make something for yourself and your son. The jar of flour will not run out and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the Lord sends rain.” The widow did as Elijah said. The jar never emptied, and the widow, Elijah and her household ate for many days.

Some time later the widow's son fell ill and stopped breathing. The widow cried out, “Man of God, did you come to remind me of my sin and to kill my son?” Elijah carried the boy up to the upper room, stretched himself out on him three times, and cried out to the Lord. The Lord heard Elijah's cry, and the boy breathed again. The widow said, “Now I know. The word of the Lord in your mouth is true.”

words.text: Don't be afraid. The jar of flour will not run out and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the Lord sends rain.
Get up, go to Zarephath in the land of Sidon, and stay there. I have commanded a widow there to feed you.
Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.

events.note: Zarephath was a village on the Mediterranean coast between Sidon and Tyre, in the land where Baal was worshiped and where Jezebel's father ruled. Jesus himself brought up this widow's story in the synagogue at Nazareth.
events.reflect: Even when I don't have enough, can I share with someone?

quiz.q: When the widow of Zarephath met Elijah, what did she have left?
options: A handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug
quiz.explain: The widow said she had nothing but a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug (1 Kgs 17:12).

img.title: The Prophet Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath
img.credit: Bernardo Strozzi, The Prophet Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath, c. 1630–1639 · Public domain

events.title: Fire on Mount Carmel
events.subtitle: The God who answers by fire
story: In the third year of the drought, all Israel gathered on Mount Carmel. The four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal were there too. Elijah stepped out before the people and said, “How long will you waver between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him; if Baal is God, follow Baal.” The people did not answer a word.

As Elijah proposed, each side would prepare a bull and lay it on the wood, and the god who answered by fire would be God. From morning on, the prophets of Baal shouted, “Baal, answer us!” At noon Elijah mocked them: “Shout louder. Maybe Baal is asleep.” They raved and cut themselves with swords and spears. But evening came, and there was no answer at all.

Elijah rebuilt the broken-down altar of the Lord with twelve stones, and had water poured on the offering three times. Elijah prayed, “Lord, let it be known today that you are the God of Israel.” Fire fell and consumed the offering, the stones, and even the water in the trench. The people fell on their faces and cried, “The Lord, he is God!” Long before, David had sung it too: the voice of the Lord strikes with flashes of fire.

words.text: How long will you waver between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him; if Baal is God, follow Baal.
Answer me, Lord, answer me, so that these people will know that you, Lord, are God, and that you are turning their hearts back again.
The Lord, he is God! The Lord, he is God!

events.note: Mount Carmel is a ridge stretching toward the Mediterranean; it is the first to catch the rain clouds coming in from the sea and was famous for always being green. It is thought to have been a place where Baal, the god of rain and plenty, was worshiped, which made it an all the more fitting place for the contest.
events.reflect: Am I torn between God and the world?

quiz.q: How many stones did Elijah use to rebuild the altar of the Lord?
quiz.explain: Elijah took twelve stones, one for each tribe descended from the sons of Jacob, and built an altar in the name of the Lord (1 Kgs 18:31–32).

img.title: Elijah's Sacrifice Consumed by Fire
img.credit: Caspar Luyken, Elijah's Sacrifice Consumed by Fire, 1712 · Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam · Public domain

events.title: A Cloud the Size of a Hand
events.subtitle: The cloud seen the seventh time
story: After the fire fell, Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink. I hear the sound of heavy rain.” The sky was still clear. While Ahab went up to eat and drink, Elijah climbed to the top of Mount Carmel and bowed down to the ground. He buried his face between his knees.

Elijah said to his servant, “Go up and look toward the sea.” The servant went and came back and said, “There is nothing there.” Elijah said, “Go back again.” The servant climbed up again and again. The seventh time, the servant came back out of breath and said, “A little cloud, as small as a man's hand, is rising from the sea.”

Elijah said to his servant, “Go and tell Ahab to hitch his horses to his chariot and go down before the rain stops him.” Soon the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain poured down. Ahab drove his chariot hard toward Jezreel. The hand of the Lord came upon Elijah, and Elijah tucked his cloak into his belt and ran through the rain ahead of the king's chariot.

words.text: Go up, eat and drink. I hear the sound of heavy rain pouring down.
Look, a little cloud, as small as a man's hand, is rising from the sea.
Go and tell Ahab to hitch his horses to his chariot and go down before the rain stops him.

events.note: From the top of Mount Carmel the Mediterranean lies in full view to the west. The road to Jezreel was nearly thirty kilometers long, and Elijah ran it ahead of the king's chariot.
events.reflect: Even when the answer is slow, do I keep praying to God?

quiz.q: On which trip did the servant see the cloud rising from the sea?
quiz.explain: Elijah told his servant to go back seven times, and the seventh time the servant saw a little cloud as small as a man's hand (1 Kgs 18:43–44).

img.title: Elijah's Servant Sees a Small Cloud
img.credit: Caspar Luyken, Elijah's Servant Sees a Small Cloud, 1712 · Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam · Public domain

events.title: Under the Broom Tree
events.subtitle: Get up and eat
story: Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done on Mount Carmel, and how he had killed the prophets of Baal with the sword. Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah to say, “May the gods punish me if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the lives of those dead prophets.” Elijah, who had called down fire from heaven, got up and fled at that one sentence from the queen.

Elijah left his servant at Beersheba, at the southern edge of Judah, and went on alone a day's journey into the wilderness. Under the blazing sun stood a single broom tree. Elijah sank down in its shade and prayed that he might die: “Lord, I have had enough. Take my life. I am no better than my ancestors.” Then he lay down under the tree and fell asleep.

Someone touched Elijah. The angel said, “Get up and eat.” By his head lay bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water. Elijah ate and drank and lay down again. The angel came back and said, “Get up and eat. The journey ahead is still long.” Strengthened by that food, Elijah walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.

words.text: Lord, I have had enough. Take my life. I am no better than my ancestors.
Get up and eat, for the journey is too long for you.
May the gods punish me severely if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of those prophets.

events.note: Beersheba was the southernmost town of Judah, a place where Jezebel, queen of northern Israel, could not easily reach. The broom tree is a desert shrub; its shade is thin, but under the blazing sun it was a precious place to rest.
events.reflect: When I am worn out and want to give up on everything, who do I lean on?

quiz.q: What lay by Elijah's head as he slept under the broom tree?
options: Bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water
quiz.explain: When Elijah woke, there by his head was bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water (1 Kgs 19:6).

img.title: Elijah Is Nourished by an Angel
img.credit: Gustave Doré, Elijah Is Nourished by an Angel, 1866 · Doré's English Bible · Public domain

events.title: The Still Small Voice at Horeb
events.subtitle: After the wind and the fire had passed
story: Elijah spent the night in a cave on Mount Horeb, and the word of the Lord came to him. The Lord asked, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” Elijah answered, “The people of Israel have rejected your covenant, torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and now they are trying to take my life too.”

The Lord said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before me.” A great and powerful wind tore the mountain apart and shattered the rocks. But the Lord was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake, and after the earthquake a fire. The Lord was not in them either. After the fire there came a low, still, small voice. Elijah covered his face with his cloak and stood at the mouth of the cave.

The Lord asked again, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” Elijah gave the same answer: “I am the only one left.” The Lord said, “Go back, and anoint Hazael king over Aram, Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha as the prophet who will succeed you. I have kept seven thousand in Israel who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”

words.text: What are you doing here, Elijah?
I have kept seven thousand in Israel, all who have not bowed the knee to Baal and have not kissed him.
The people of Israel have rejected your covenant, torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and they are trying to take my life too.

events.note: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, where Moses stood before the burning bush and received the law. It lies hundreds of kilometers south of Beersheba, and there are several views about its exact location.
events.reflect: Do I treat only what I want to hear as God's will?

quiz.q: How many people did the Lord say he had kept who had not bowed the knee to Baal?
quiz.explain: The Lord said he had kept seven thousand in Israel who had not bowed the knee to Baal or kissed him (1 Kgs 19:18).

img.title: Elijah in the Cave
img.credit: Jan Luyken, Elijah in the Cave, 1704 · Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam · Public domain

events.title: The Cloak Thrown over Elisha
events.subtitle: The day he burned the yoke
story: The fields of Abel-meholah in the Jordan Valley were full of the breathing of oxen pulling plows. Twelve pairs of oxen turned the soil in a line, and Elisha son of Shaphat was driving the twelfth pair, at the very end. Elijah, back from Mount Horeb, came walking to the edge of that field.

As Elijah passed by Elisha, he threw his cloak over him. Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah and said, “Let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you.” Elijah said, “Go back. What have I done to you?”

Elisha went back. Then he slaughtered the pair of oxen he had been driving. He broke up the plow and the yoke to make a fire, boiled the meat, and gave it to the people. He left no yoke to put on again and no plow to come back to. Elisha got up, followed Elijah, and served him.

words.text: Let me kiss my father and mother goodbye. Then I will follow you.
Go back. What have I done to you?
Anoint Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to be the prophet who will succeed you.

events.note: A prophet's cloak marked who he was, and throwing it over someone is understood as a call to carry on his work. Twelve pairs meant twenty-four oxen, which shows that Elisha's family had a well-off farm.
events.reflect: What do I need to let go of now in order to follow the Lord?

quiz.q: What was Elisha doing when Elijah threw his cloak over him?
quiz.explain: Elisha was plowing with twelve pairs of oxen ahead of him, and he was with the twelfth pair (1 Kgs 19:19).

img.title: The Calling of Elisha
img.credit: Jan Matsys, The Calling of Elisha, 1572 · Public domain

events.title: Naboth's Vineyard
events.subtitle: The prophet waiting in a stolen vineyard
story: Right beside the palace in Jezreel was Naboth's vineyard. King Ahab said to Naboth, “Give me your vineyard. I want it for a vegetable garden. I will give you a better vineyard for it, or pay you what it is worth.” Naboth answered, “The Lord forbids me to give you the land I inherited from my ancestors.” Ahab went home sullen, lay on his bed with his face turned away, and would not eat.

Ahab's wife Jezebel said, “Aren't you the one who rules Israel now? I will get you that vineyard.” Jezebel wrote letters in the king's name and sealed them with the king's seal. Where a fast had been proclaimed, two worthless men stood up and gave false testimony: “Naboth has cursed God and the king.” Naboth was dragged outside the city and stoned to death.

When Ahab went down to take the vineyard, Elijah was standing there. Ahab said, “So you have found me, my enemy?” Elijah said, “I have found you. In the place where dogs licked up Naboth's blood, dogs will lick up your blood too.” Ahab tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and fasted. The Lord saw how Ahab had humbled himself and put off the disaster on his house until his son's day.

words.text: Have you murdered a man and taken his land as well? In the place where dogs licked up Naboth's blood, dogs will lick up your blood too.
I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the Lord's eyes.
The Lord forbids me to give you the land I inherited from my ancestors.
Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the disaster in his day.

events.note: In Israel each family's land was an inheritance received from God, and it could not simply be sold off. Jezreel, like Samaria, was a royal city where Ahab stayed, on a hill overlooking the broad Valley of Jezreel.
events.reflect: Is my greed making me take lightly what belongs to others?

quiz.q: Why did Naboth refuse to give his vineyard to Ahab?
options: He had already sold it to someone else
It was the inheritance of his ancestors
quiz.explain: Naboth answered that the Lord forbade him to give the inheritance of his ancestors to the king (1 Kgs 21:3).

img.title: Jezebel and Ahab Meeting Elijah in Naboth's Vineyard
img.credit: Frank Dicksee, Jezebel and Ahab Meeting Elijah in Naboth's Vineyard · Public domain

events.title: Micaiah Stands Alone
events.subtitle: Four hundred against one
story: On the threshing floor by the gate of Samaria, two kings sat side by side in their royal robes. They were Ahab king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah. They were about to set out together to take Ramoth-gilead back from Aram. Four hundred prophets cried out with one voice, “Go up. The Lord will give the city into the king's hand.”

Jehoshaphat asked, “Is there no other prophet of the Lord here?” Ahab answered, “There is Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him. He never prophesies anything good about me.” The official sent to fetch Micaiah whispered to him, “Speak favorably, like the other prophets.” Micaiah answered, “I will say only what the Lord tells me.”

Micaiah said before the king, “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd.” The prophet Zedekiah struck Micaiah on the cheek, and Ahab had Micaiah thrown into prison. Ahab went into battle in disguise. But an arrow shot at random pierced Ahab's armor between its joints. That evening Ahab died, and when his chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria, dogs licked up his blood. It happened just as the Lord had said.

words.text: As surely as the Lord lives, I will say only what the Lord tells me.
I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd.
If you come back safely, the Lord has not spoken through me.
First ask for the word of the Lord today.

events.note: Ramoth-gilead was a fortress town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, which Aram and Israel fought over many times. Jehoshaphat king of Judah married his son to Ahab's daughter Athaliah, so the two kings were joined by marriage.
events.reflect: Even when everyone says the same thing, can I follow God's word?

quiz.q: Why did Ahab say he hated Micaiah?
options: He never prophesied anything good about Ahab
He stole treasure from the palace
quiz.explain: Ahab said he hated Micaiah because he never prophesied anything good about him, only bad (1 Kgs 22:8).

img.title: The Prophet Micaiah before Jehoshaphat and Ahab
img.credit: Caspar Luyken, The Prophet Micaiah before Jehoshaphat and Ahab, 1712 · Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam · Public domain

events.title: Chariot of Fire and Whirlwind
events.subtitle: Picking up the fallen cloak
story: Elijah set out from Gilgal with Elisha. Elijah said, “Stay here. The Lord is sending me to Bethel.” Elisha answered, “As surely as the Lord lives and as you live, I will not leave you.” At Bethel and again at Jericho the same words passed between them. To the very end, Elisha would not leave his master's side.

When they reached the Jordan, fifty men from the company of the prophets stood at a distance and watched. Elijah rolled up his cloak and struck the water, the water parted, and the two of them crossed over on dry ground. Elijah asked, “What can I do for you before I am taken from you?” Elisha said, “Let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” Elijah said, “You have asked a hard thing.”

As they walked along talking, a chariot of fire and horses of fire came between the two of them. Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha cried out, “My father, my father!” Elisha picked up Elijah's fallen cloak, struck the water of the Jordan with it and cried, “Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?” The water parted. The prophets' disciples said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.”

words.text: Let a double portion of your spirit be on me.
You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be yours; but if you do not see me, it will not.
My father, my father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!
Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?

events.note: A double portion echoes the law by which the firstborn son received two shares of his father's inheritance, so the request is understood as asking to become Elijah's firstborn heir. Elijah is remembered, like Enoch, as one who went to heaven without seeing death.
events.reflect: Is there someone I need to stand by to the very end?

quiz.q: After they crossed the Jordan, what did Elisha ask Elijah for?
options: A double portion of Elijah's spirit
quiz.explain: Elisha asked for a double portion of Elijah's spirit to be on him (2 Kgs 2:9).

img.title: Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire
img.credit: Giuseppe Angeli, Elijah Taken Up in a Chariot of Fire, c. 1740–1755 · National Gallery of Art, Washington · Public domain

events.title: The Shunammite Woman's Son
events.subtitle: A gift she never asked for, a son given back
story: As the sun went down over the fields of Shunem, a tired traveler passed by a certain house. It was Elisha, the man of God. A well-to-do woman of that house urged him to stay and eat every time he came by. The woman said to her husband, “That man is a holy man of God. Let's build a small room on the roof and put a bed, a table, a chair and a lamp in it.”

Elisha's servant Gehazi said quietly, “This woman has no son, and her husband is old.” Elisha said to the woman, who was standing in the doorway, “About this time next year you will hold a son in your arms.” The woman trembled and said, “Man of God, do not deceive your servant.” At that time the next year, a son really was born to her.

The child grew, and one day he went out to his father among the reapers. The boy cried out to his father, “My head! My head hurts!” The father told a servant to carry the boy to his mother. The boy lay on his mother's lap until noon, and then he died. The woman laid her son on the prophet's bed, rushed to Mount Carmel and took hold of Elisha's feet. Elisha went into that room, shut the door, prayed, and stretched himself out on the boy. The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.

words.text: About this time next year you will hold a son in your arms.
Did I ever ask you for a son, my lord? Didn't I tell you not to deceive me?
Pick up your son.

events.note: Shunem was a village at the foot of the Hill of Moreh, on the north side of the Valley of Jezreel. Mount Carmel, where Elisha was staying, lay about twenty-five kilometers to the west even at its nearest slopes, so the woman probably rode a donkey for half a day.
events.reflect: Have I ever warmly welcomed someone without expecting anything in return?

quiz.q: After Elisha prayed, what did the Shunammite woman's son do before he opened his eyes?
quiz.explain: When Elisha stretched himself out on the boy, the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes (2 Kgs 4:35).

img.title: Elisha and the Shunammite Woman on Mount Carmel
img.credit: Gerbrand van den Eeckhout, Elisha and the Shunammite Woman on Mount Carmel, 1649 · National Museum in Warsaw · Public domain

events.title: Naaman's Seven Times
events.subtitle: The Jordan where a great general was humbled
story: Naaman, commander of the army of Aram, was a great warrior whom his king valued highly, but he had leprosy. In his house a young girl taken captive from Israel served Naaman's wife. The girl said to her mistress, “If only my master would see the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his disease.”

Naaman came with his horses and chariots, loaded with silver and gold, and stopped at the door of Elisha's house. Elisha did not even come out, but sent a messenger to say, “Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan.” Naaman turned away in anger and said, “I thought he would surely come out, wave his hand and heal me. Aren't the rivers of Damascus better than the waters of this land?”

Naaman's servants came to him and calmed him: “If the prophet had told you to do some great thing, wouldn't you have done it? Why not do it when he only says, Wash?” Naaman went down to the Jordan and dipped himself in the water seven times. When he rose from the water the seventh time, his skin was clean, like the skin of a young child. Naaman went back to Elisha and said, “Now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.”

words.text: Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan. Then your skin will be restored, and you will be clean.
Now I know that there is no God in all the world except in Israel.
If only my master would see the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy.
As surely as the Lord lives, whom I serve, I will not accept anything.

events.note: The rivers of Damascus that Naaman compared, the Abana and the Pharpar, were clear rivers flowing down from the Anti-Lebanon range and Mount Hermon. The lower Jordan, by comparison, is a narrow, winding, muddy-colored river.
events.reflect: Is there some small thing I am not obeying because of my pride?

quiz.q: How many times did Elisha tell Naaman to wash in the Jordan?
quiz.explain: Elisha said that if Naaman went and washed seven times in the Jordan, his skin would be restored and he would be clean (2 Kgs 5:10, 14).

img.title: Elisha Refusing Naaman's Gifts
img.credit: Lambert Jacobsz, Elisha Refusing Naaman's Gifts, c. 1628–1633 · The Leiden Collection, New York · Public domain

events.title: The Axe Head That Floated
events.subtitle: One borrowed iron axe
story: The disciples of the prophets said to Elisha, “The place where we live with you is too small for us. Let's go to the Jordan, each cut a beam, and build a place to live there.” Elisha told them to go, and one of the disciples said, “Please come with us.” Elisha agreed and went along. Soon the sound of axes rang through the woods by the Jordan.

As one of the disciples was cutting down a tree, the iron axe head flew off the handle and fell into the water. The disciple cried out, “Oh no, master, it was borrowed!” Iron was precious in those days. For the disciple who had lost what he borrowed, that axe was a debt he had no way to repay.

Elisha asked, “Where did it fall?” The disciple pointed to the place. Elisha cut a stick and threw it there. Then the iron axe head that had sunk floated up to the surface. Elisha said, “Pick it up.” The disciple reached out his hand and took hold of the floating axe head.

words.text: Where did it fall?
Pick it up.
Oh no, master, it was a borrowed axe!

events.note: Iron was spreading widely in those days, but iron tools were still expensive. The law said that if a borrowed animal was injured or died, the borrower had to make it good.
events.reflect: What worry have I kept from God because it seemed too small?

quiz.q: How did the iron axe head that fell into the water come back up?
options: Elisha put his hand in the water
Elisha struck the water with his cloak
Elisha cut a stick and threw it in
quiz.explain: Elisha cut a stick and threw it into the place, and the iron axe head floated (2 Kgs 6:6).

img.title: Elisha Makes the Axe Swim
img.credit: Unknown artist, Elisha Makes the Axe Swim, 1873 · The Story of the Bible from Genesis to Revelation · Public domain

events.title: Horses and Chariots of Fire around Dothan
events.subtitle: An army of fire seen with opened eyes
story: The king of Aram secretly chose places to camp so he could strike Israel, but each time the king of Israel knew ahead of time and avoided them. The king of Aram asked his officers, “Which of you is on the side of the king of Israel?” One of his officers answered, “None of us, my lord. The prophet Elisha tells the king of Israel even the words you speak in your bedroom.”

When the king of Aram heard that Elisha was in Dothan, he sent horses and chariots and a great army by night and surrounded the city. Elisha's servant went out at dawn and cried, “Oh, my master, what shall we do?” Elisha said, “Don't be afraid. Those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Elisha prayed, “Lord, open this young man's eyes so that he may see.”

The servant's eyes were opened, and the hills all around Elisha were full of horses and chariots of fire. Elisha prayed again, and the eyes of the Aramean soldiers were darkened. Elisha led them to Samaria, stopped the king of Israel from striking them down, and had them fed and sent home. What the servant felt that day as he looked around the hills was like the song the pilgrims sang in later years. That song goes like this: my help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.

words.text: Don't be afraid. Those who are with us are more than those who are with them.
Lord, open this young man's eyes so that he may see.
Do not strike them down. Set bread and water before them so they can eat and drink, and then send them back to their master.

events.note: Dothan was a hill town north of Samaria, on the road that crosses over into the Valley of Jezreel. It was also near Dothan that Joseph was sold by his brothers.
events.reflect: Am I so focused on the threat in front of me that I forget God is with me?

quiz.q: When the servant's eyes were opened, what filled the hills around Elisha?
quiz.explain: The Lord opened the servant's eyes, and the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha (2 Kgs 6:17).

img.title: Elisha at Dothan
img.credit: Providence Lithograph Company, Elisha at Dothan, 1898 · Public domain

events.title: Four Lepers outside the Gate
events.subtitle: Good news carried from the edge of death
story: When the Aramean army besieged Samaria, the hunger in the city grew so bad that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver. Elisha said, “This is the word of the Lord: About this time tomorrow, at the city gate, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel.” The king's officer sneered, “Even if the Lord opened windows in the sky, could such a thing happen?” Elisha answered, “You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it.”

Four men with leprosy were sitting at the entrance of the city gate. They said to one another, “Why sit here until we die? Let's go over to the Aramean camp. If they spare us, we live; if they kill us, we die.” When they reached the camp at dusk, it was empty. The Lord had made the Aramean army hear the sound of chariots of a great army, and they had left their tents and fled.

The four men ate and drank and were hiding silver and gold when suddenly they stopped. They said to one another, “What we are doing is wrong. This is a day of good news, and we are keeping quiet.” When the people heard the news, they poured out to the camp, and a seah of flour sold for a shekel. The officer who had sneered at Elisha was keeping the gate when the people trampled him to death.

words.text: Hear the word of the Lord: About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will be bought and sold for a shekel.
What we are doing is not right. This is a day of good news, and we are keeping our mouths shut.
You will see it with your own eyes, but you will not eat any of it.

events.note: Under the law, people with leprosy had to live apart, outside the camp, so these men stayed outside the city gate. A seah was a measure of grain of about seven liters, and a shekel is thought to have been about eleven grams of silver.
events.reflect: What good news should I pass on instead of keeping it to myself?

quiz.q: Why did the Aramean army abandon its camp and flee?
options: The Lord made them hear the sound of a great army's chariots
The lepers set it on fire
quiz.explain: The Lord made the Aramean army hear the sound of chariots and horses and a great army, and they fled at dusk (2 Kgs 7:6–7).

img.title: The People of Samaria Plunder the Abandoned Syrian Camp

events.title: Jehu's Wild Ride
events.subtitle: The chariot of judgment that came driving like a madman
story: Elisha called one of the disciples of the prophets and said, “Take this flask of oil and go to Ramoth-gilead. Take Jehu, the grandson of Nimshi, into an inner room, pour oil on his head, then open the door and run.” The young prophet called Jehu out from among the commanders, went into the house, poured the oil on his head and said, “This is what the Lord says: You are to strike down the house of Ahab.” Then the young prophet opened the door and ran.

The commanders blew the trumpet and shouted, “Jehu is king!” Jehu drove his chariot hard toward Jezreel. The watchman on the tower called out, “The driving is like the driving of Jehu; he drives like a madman.” Joram the king, Ahab's son, came out and asked, “Is it peace, Jehu?” Jehu answered, “How can there be peace, while the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel are so many?” Jehu's arrow pierced Joram through.

Ahab's wife Jezebel painted her eyes, arranged her hair and stood at the window. Jezebel said to Jehu as he came in through the gate, “Is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?” Jehu looked up at the window and shouted, “Who is on my side?” At Jehu's command, the officials threw Jezebel out of the window. Elijah's word that dogs would devour Jezebel in the land of Jezreel later came true exactly.

words.text: I anoint you king over my people Israel. You are to strike down the house of your master Ahab.
Pour the oil on his head, then open the door and run. Do not wait.
How can there be any peace, while the idolatry and witchcraft of your mother Jezebel are so many?
This is the word the Lord spoke through Elijah: In the land of Jezreel dogs will eat the flesh of Jezebel.

events.note: Jezreel had a second palace of Ahab's royal house, and beside it lay Naboth's vineyard, which Ahab had seized. Jehu had Joram's body thrown onto that very field of Naboth.
events.reflect: Even when evil seems to hold power for a long time, do I believe in God's justice?

quiz.q: What told the watchman on the tower that Jehu was coming?
options: The way he drove his chariot like a madman
quiz.explain: The watchman reported that the driving was like a madman's, like that of Jehu grandson of Nimshi (2 Kgs 9:20).

events.title: Joash, the Child Hidden in the Temple
events.subtitle: David's lamp, almost put out
story: When Ahaziah king of Judah died, his mother Athaliah rose up and killed the whole royal family. On the day the sword swept through the palace, Ahaziah's sister Jehosheba secretly took her baby nephew Joash and hid him with his nurse in a bedroom. For the next six years the child grew up hidden in the temple of the Lord, while Athaliah ruled the land.

In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada called the commanders of hundreds to the temple, put them under oath and showed them the king's son. Jehoiada handed out to them the spears and shields that had belonged to King David. The guards stood with weapons in hand along both sides of the temple. Jehoiada brought out the boy, put the crown on him and anointed him. The people clapped their hands and shouted, “Long live the king!”

Athaliah heard the shouting and came into the temple. When she saw the young king standing by the pillar and the people blowing trumpets, Athaliah tore her clothes and screamed, “Treason! Treason!” Jehoiada gave the order: “Do not put her to death inside the temple.” Athaliah was dragged out and put to death, and the people tore down the temple of Baal. Seven-year-old Joash sat on the throne of David.

words.text: Bring Athaliah out between the ranks. Strike down with the sword anyone who follows her. Do not put her to death inside the temple of the Lord.
Treason! Treason!
Long live the king!

events.note: Second Chronicles tells us that Jehosheba was the wife of Jehoiada the priest. Athaliah came from Ahab's house in northern Israel and married into Judah, and she brought Baal worship into Jerusalem.
events.reflect: Even if no one notices, can I step up to protect someone?

quiz.q: How long did Joash stay hidden in the temple before he became king?
quiz.explain: Joash was hidden in the temple of the Lord for six years, and in the seventh year Jehoiada made him king (2 Kgs 11:3–4).

events.title: Elisha's Last Arrows
events.subtitle: The arrows that stopped at three
story: The aged Elisha lay ill with the sickness that would end his life. Joash king of northern Israel came to see him and wept over his face. He was a king of the north who had the same name as Joash king of Judah, the boy who grew up hidden in the temple. Joash cried out, “My father, my father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!” They were the very words Elisha had cried long ago as he watched Elijah go up to heaven.

Elisha said, “Get a bow and some arrows.” When the king took hold of the bow, Elisha put his own hands on the king's hands. Elisha said, “Open the east window and shoot.” As the arrow flew out the window, Elisha cried, “The Lord's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram! You will strike Aram at Aphek.”

Elisha said again, “Take the arrows and strike the ground.” The king struck three times and stopped. Elisha was angry and said, “You should have struck five or six times. Then you would have destroyed Aram completely, but now you will defeat it only three times.” Elisha died and was buried. Later a dead man was thrown into Elisha's tomb, and when the body touched Elisha's bones, the man came to life and stood up.

words.text: You should have struck five or six times. Then you would have struck Aram down to the end, but now you will defeat it only three times.
This is the Lord's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram.
My father, my father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!

events.note: Elisha is thought to have served as a prophet for more than fifty years, from the time of Ahab's son Joram to the time of Jehu's grandson Joash. Afterward Joash defeated Aram three times and won back the towns that had been taken.
events.reflect: While asking for God's help, am I giving up too easily?

quiz.q: How many times did King Joash strike the ground with the arrows?
quiz.explain: When Joash struck three times and stopped, Elisha was angry and said he should have struck five or six times (2 Kgs 13:18–19).

events.title: The Fall of Samaria
events.subtitle: The last day of a nation that would not listen
story: For the third year running, the watchman on the wall of Samaria looked down on the same sight. The Assyrian army had the city surrounded. Hoshea son of Elah, the last king of northern Israel, had stopped paying the yearly tribute to Assyria and secretly asked the king of Egypt for help, but he was found out and thrown into prison. Even after the king was taken away, the city held out for three years.

In the ninth year of Hoshea's reign, Samaria finally fell. The king of Assyria took the people of Israel captive and carried them off to a faraway land. They were taken to Halah, to the banks of the Habor River in the region of Gozan, and to the towns of the Medes. Of the two kingdoms that had split apart after Solomon's death, Israel in the north came to its end in this way.

All that time the Lord had sent prophets again and again to say, “Turn from your evil ways and keep my commands.” But the people were stubborn and would not listen. They served the golden calves Jeroboam had made, and Baal, and they even burned their own children in the fire as offerings to idols. In the end the Lord drove Israel out of the land, and only the tribe of Judah was left.

words.text: Turn from your evil ways. Keep my commands and decrees, according to the whole law I commanded your ancestors and sent to you through my servants the prophets.
Do not serve other gods.

events.note: Samaria fell around 722 BC. Kings records that Shalmaneser besieged the city and says only that “the king of Assyria” captured it, but Assyrian records say that Sargon II, who followed Shalmaneser V, took the city and carried off more than twenty-seven thousand people.
events.reflect: What word from God have I heard again and again but still not followed?

quiz.q: Who was king of northern Israel when Samaria fell?
quiz.explain: In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria and carried Israel off into captivity (2 Kgs 17:6).

events.title: The King Who Smashed the Bronze Snake
events.subtitle: Breaking what everyone bowed to
story: Incense smoke curled around a snake made of bronze. People bowed down before it and burned incense. It was the very snake Moses was said to have lifted up on a pole in the wilderness, long, long ago. Hezekiah, who had become king of Judah at twenty-five, stood before it. He was the son of King Ahaz, but Hezekiah was a king who had chosen to follow the way of his ancestor David rather than the way of his father.

First Hezekiah tore down the high places. He smashed the sacred pillars and cut down the Asherah poles. Then he came to the bronze snake. It had once been a sign that saved Israel's life, but now it had become a thing people bowed down to instead of God. Hezekiah broke the bronze snake to pieces and called it Nehushtan. The name is usually taken to mean a piece of bronze.

Hezekiah trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel. Among the kings of Judah, none before him or after him was like him. Hezekiah held fast to the Lord and did not turn away, and the Lord was with him, and wherever he went he succeeded. At last Hezekiah turned his back on the mighty Assyrian empire and refused to serve it any longer. Dark clouds began to gather in the northern sky.

words.text: Hezekiah trusted in the Lord, the God of Israel. Among all the kings of Judah, none who came before him and none who came after him was like him.
He broke to pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, because until then the people of Israel had been burning incense to it. He called it Nehushtan.
He held fast to the Lord and did not turn away, and he kept the commands the Lord had given Moses. The Lord was with him, and wherever he went he succeeded.

events.note: The bronze snake was made by Moses in Numbers 21 to save the people who had been bitten by fiery serpents. In Hebrew the name Nehushtan calls to mind both “bronze” and “snake,” and it is sometimes explained as meaning “a piece of bronze.”
events.reflect: Even if I have held on to something for a long time, can I let it go if it comes before God?

quiz.q: What name did Hezekiah give the bronze snake when he broke it?
quiz.explain: Because the people of Israel had been burning incense to the bronze snake until then, Hezekiah broke it to pieces and called it Nehushtan (2 Kgs 18:4).

events.title: The Rabshakeh's Taunts
events.subtitle: What are you trusting in?
story: Beside the channel of the Upper Pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field, a great Assyrian army stood in ranks. These were the Tartan, the Rabsaris and the Rabshakeh, commanders sent from Lachish by Sennacherib king of Assyria. From inside the city came Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the secretary and Joah the recorder. On the wall above, the people stood packed together, holding their breath.

The Rabshakeh spoke in a loud voice: “What are you trusting in, that you hold out like this? Egypt is a broken reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it. Will you say you trust in the Lord? Isn't he the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah tore down?” Eliakim, Shebna and Joah pleaded urgently, “Speak in Aramaic. The people on the wall are listening.” Instead the Rabshakeh shouted even louder in Hebrew.

The Rabshakeh shouted, “Don't let Hezekiah deceive you. Did the gods of Hamath and Arpad save their lands? Has any god saved Samaria from my hand? How then can the Lord save Jerusalem?” The wall was silent. The king had commanded them not to answer. Eliakim and the officials went back to Hezekiah with their clothes torn.

words.text: What are you trusting in, that you hold out like this? You are leaning on Egypt, that broken reed. Anyone who leans on it gets his hand pierced through.
Which of all the gods of the nations has saved its land from my hand? How then can the Lord save Jerusalem from my hand?
Please speak in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak in Hebrew where the people on the wall can hear.
Do not answer him a single word.

events.note: At this time Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked the fortified towns of Judah and captured Lachish. A large relief showing the assault on Lachish survives from the walls of the palace at Nineveh.
events.reflect: Do I trust God's promise more than people's mockery?

quiz.q: In what language did Eliakim ask the Rabshakeh to speak?
quiz.explain: He asked him to speak in Aramaic so the people on the wall could not understand, but the Rabshakeh shouted even louder in Hebrew (2 Kgs 18:26–28).

events.title: A Letter Spread Out in the Temple
events.subtitle: Laying it all out before God
story: Hezekiah tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and went into the temple. Then he sent his officials and the senior priests to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz with this message: “Today is a day of distress and disgrace. It is as if a child has come to the moment of birth, and there is no strength to deliver it.” Isaiah answered, “This is what the Lord says: Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have insulted me.”

Soon afterward a letter came from the king of Assyria. The letter said, “Don't let the god you trust in deceive you.” Hezekiah took the letter up to the temple and spread it out just as it was before the Lord. Hezekiah prayed, “Lord, enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. The gods they burned were only wood and stone, shaped by human hands. Now save us.”

Isaiah sent word to Hezekiah: “This is what the Lord says: I have heard your prayer. The king of Assyria will not enter this city or shoot a single arrow here; he will go back the way he came. I will defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.” A song in praise of Zion sings it this way: as we have heard, so now we have seen; God will make this city stand firm forever.

words.text: The king of Assyria will not enter this city or shoot a single arrow here. I will defend this city and save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.
This is what the Lord says: Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have insulted me.
Lord, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. Now save us, so that all the world may know that you alone are God.

events.note: The cherubim were two winged figures spread over the lid of the ark of the covenant, and they were seen as the throne of the invisible God. Isaiah 36–37 tells the same story almost word for word.
events.reflect: What worry do I need to spread out before God right now and leave with him?

quiz.q: What did Hezekiah do when he received the letter from the king of Assyria?
options: He went up to the temple and spread it out before the Lord
quiz.explain: Hezekiah read the letter, went up to the temple of the Lord, spread it out before the Lord and prayed (2 Kgs 19:14–15).

events.title: Night in the Assyrian Camp
events.subtitle: What happened in a single night
story: That night Jerusalem held its breath. The great Assyrian army was still camped in the land of Judah, and the only thing the people in the city had to hold on to was the word Isaiah had brought them. The Lord had said, “The king of Assyria will not enter this city; he will go back the way he came.” Holding on to that one word, the people stayed awake through the long night.

That very night the angel of the Lord went out and struck the Assyrian camp. When people got up early in the morning, a hundred and eighty-five thousand soldiers never rose again. The army that had seemed ready to swallow Judah collapsed in a single night. Only a heavy silence settled over the camp.

Sennacherib king of Assyria withdrew his army and went back to Nineveh. Later, while Sennacherib was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, two of his sons killed him, and another son, Esarhaddon, became king. One of the psalms sings it this way: be still, and know that I am God.

words.text: That night the angel of the Lord went out and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. When people got up early in the morning, they were all dead bodies.
He will go back the way he came, and he will not enter this city. This is what the Lord says.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp, went home, and stayed in Nineveh.

events.note: Sennacherib's chronicle prism says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem “like a bird in a cage,” but it says nothing about capturing the city. Sennacherib was murdered by his sons around 681 BC.
events.reflect: Am I trying to fix everything on my own and forgetting to pray?

quiz.q: How many Assyrian soldiers did the angel of the Lord strike down that night?
quiz.explain: The angel of the Lord struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp (2 Kgs 19:35).

events.title: The Shadow That Went Back
events.subtitle: Tears turned to the wall
story: Hezekiah fell ill and was about to die. The prophet Isaiah came and said, “This is what the Lord says: Put your house in order. You are going to die; you will not recover.” Hezekiah turned his face to the wall. Hezekiah prayed, “Lord, remember how I have walked before you faithfully and with a whole heart.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.

Before Isaiah had even left the middle court of the palace, the word of the Lord came to him. The Lord said, “Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. I will heal you. On the third day you will go up to the temple. I will add fifteen years to your life.”

Isaiah had a paste of figs put on the king's boil, and the king recovered. Hezekiah asked, “What will be the sign that the Lord will heal me?” Isaiah asked, “Do you want the shadow to go forward ten steps, or to go back ten steps?” Hezekiah answered, “Let it go back.” Isaiah cried out to the Lord, and the shadow that had fallen on the stairway of Ahaz went back ten steps.

words.text: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. I will heal you. I will add fifteen years to your life.
This is what the Lord says: Put your house in order. You are going to die; you will not recover.
Lord, remember how I have walked before you faithfully and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your eyes.

events.note: The “stairway of Ahaz” was a stairway built by King Ahaz, which is thought to have worked as a sundial, measuring time by the sun's shadow. Isaiah 38 includes the song of thanks Hezekiah wrote after he recovered.
events.reflect: When things are hardest, who is the one I turn to first?

quiz.q: As a sign, what happened to the sun's shadow on the stairway of Ahaz?
quiz.explain: Hezekiah asked for the shadow to go back, and when Isaiah cried out to the Lord, the shadow went back ten steps (2 Kgs 20:10–11).

events.title: Treasures Shown to the Envoys from Babylon
events.subtitle: Every storehouse thrown open
story: Envoys from faraway Babylon came into Jerusalem carrying letters and gifts. They had been sent by Merodach-baladan king of Babylon, who had heard that Hezekiah was ill. A king from a distant land had sent people to ask after his health. Hezekiah was delighted and listened to what the envoys had to say.

Hezekiah took the envoys to his treasure house. One by one he opened up the silver and the gold, the spices and the fine oil, and even his armory. There was nothing in his palace or in all his kingdom that he did not show them. The envoys' eyes searched every corner of the storerooms. Then the prophet Isaiah came to see the king.

Isaiah asked, “Where did those men come from, and what did they see?” Hezekiah answered, “They came from faraway Babylon, and they saw everything in my storehouses.” Isaiah gave him the word of the Lord: “The day is coming when everything in this palace, and all that your ancestors stored up, will be carried off to Babylon. Some of the sons who will be born to you will be taken away and become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” Hezekiah said, “The word of the Lord you have spoken is good. At least there will be peace while I live.”

words.text: Hear the word of the Lord: The day is coming when everything in this palace and all that your ancestors stored up will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left.
They saw everything in my palace. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them.
The word of the Lord you have spoken is good. Won't there be peace and security as long as I live?

events.note: Merodach-baladan was a Chaldean who seized the throne of Babylon twice in defiance of Assyria, and this embassy is thought to have been a search for allies against Assyria.
events.reflect: Does my wish to be recognized by people make me forget God?

quiz.q: Which country did the envoys come from, to whom Hezekiah showed his treasure house?
quiz.explain: They were envoys sent by Merodach-baladan king of Babylon, and Hezekiah showed them his whole treasure house (2 Kgs 20:12–15).
