events.title: The Book of the Law Found in the Temple
events.subtitle: Clothes torn before the word
story: While the temple was being repaired, King Josiah sent Shaphan the secretary to the temple. The high priest Hilkiah said to Shaphan, “I have found the Book of the Law in the temple of the Lord.” Shaphan read the book and brought it to the palace. Josiah had become king at eight and was now in the eighteenth year of his reign, and before him Shaphan read the book aloud.

As Josiah listened to the words of the law, he tore his clothes. Josiah gave an order: “Go and ask the Lord for me, for the people and for all Judah about the words of this book. The Lord's anger is great, because our ancestors did not listen to these words.” Hilkiah, Shaphan and the others went to the prophetess Huldah, who lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem.

Huldah said, “This is what the Lord says: Because this people has forsaken me, I will bring disaster on this place. But tell the king of Judah: Because your heart was tender when you heard these words, and you tore your clothes and wept, I have heard you too. Your eyes will not see that disaster.” Josiah read the Book of the Covenant before all the people and made a covenant to follow the Lord.

words.text: Because your heart was tender when you heard these words, and you humbled yourself before the Lord, tore your clothes and wept, I have heard you too. This is what the Lord says.
I have found the Book of the Law in the temple of the Lord.
Go and ask the Lord for me, for the people and for all Judah about the words of this book. His anger is great, because our ancestors did not obey these words.

events.note: The Book of the Law found at this time is thought to have been Deuteronomy, or its central part. The “Second Quarter” where Huldah lived is believed to be the new district on the west side of Jerusalem, added around Hezekiah's time.
events.reflect: When God's word exposes my wrongs, do I turn back instead of making excuses?

quiz.q: Which prophet did Josiah's officials go to, to ask the Lord about the words of the Book of the Law?
quiz.explain: Hilkiah, Shaphan and the others went to the prophetess Huldah, who lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 22:14).

events.title: Death at Megiddo
events.subtitle: The sudden end of the most faithful king
story: Passover songs rang through Jerusalem. Josiah gave the command: “Keep the Passover to the Lord your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant.” No Passover like it had been kept since the days of the judges. Josiah got rid of all the mediums, the fortune-tellers and the idols. No king before him or after him turned to the Lord with all his heart and all his strength as Josiah did.

Even so, the Lord did not turn away from the fierce anger that had been kindled by the sins of Josiah's grandfather Manasseh. The Lord said, “I will remove Judah from my presence as I removed Israel. I will reject Jerusalem, this city I chose, and this temple, where I said my name would be.”

At that time Neco king of Egypt was marching up to the Euphrates River to help the king of Assyria. When Josiah went out to Megiddo to block his way, Neco sent messengers to warn Josiah that God had told Neco to hurry, so Josiah should not stand in his way. But Josiah would not listen; he went out to fight in disguise, and the arrows of the Egyptian archers badly wounded him. His officials moved the king to another chariot and brought him to Jerusalem, but Josiah died there, and all Judah and Jeremiah mourned for him. The people anointed Josiah's son Jehoahaz and made him king.

words.text: I will remove Judah from my presence as I removed Israel. I will reject Jerusalem, this city I chose, and this temple, where I said my name would be.
Neither before Josiah nor after him was there a king who turned to the Lord as he did, with all his heart, all his soul and all his strength, according to the whole law of Moses.
Keep the Passover to the Lord your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant.
God has told me to hurry. Stop opposing God, who is with me, and stand aside, or he will destroy you.

events.note: Megiddo was a fortress guarding the pass where the coastal road enters the Valley of Jezreel. Neco was on his way to help Assyria against Babylon, and 2 Chronicles 35 says that Josiah fought in disguise and was struck by arrows.
events.reflect: Do I ever rush ahead, trusting only my own judgment without asking God's will?

quiz.q: Where did Josiah die when he went out against Neco king of Egypt?
quiz.explain: Pharaoh Neco faced Josiah at Megiddo and killed him (2 Kgs 23:29).

events.title: The Temple in Flames
events.subtitle: The house of the Name falls in the fire
story: On the tenth day of the tenth month of King Zedekiah's ninth year, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with his whole army and surrounded Jerusalem. Siege ramps were built all around the city. The siege lasted until the eleventh year. By the ninth day of the fourth month, there was no food left in the city. At last the wall was broken through.

That night Zedekiah and his soldiers slipped out through the gate between the two walls, by the king's garden, and fled toward the Arabah. The Babylonian army chased them, caught the king on the plains of Jericho, and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah. The king of Babylon killed Zedekiah's sons before his eyes, then put out Zedekiah's eyes, bound him in bronze chains and took him to Babylon.

On the seventh day of the fifth month, Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard, came and burned the temple of the Lord, the palace and all the great houses. The bronze pillars and the bronze Sea were broken up and carried off to Babylon. The people were taken captive, and only the poorest were left to look after the vineyards and fields. Over the ruined sanctuary a song burst out: How long, O God? They have set your sanctuary on fire.

words.text: He burned the temple of the Lord, the palace and every house in Jerusalem. Every great house was burned to the ground.
I will wipe Jerusalem clean as someone wipes a dish and turns it upside down. I will abandon those of my people who are left and hand them over to their enemies.
So Judah was taken captive and went away from its own land.

events.note: Solomon's temple fell nearly four hundred years after it was built. Some date its fall to 586 BC and others to 587 BC. To this day Jewish people fast on the ninth day of the month of Av to remember the destruction of the temple.
events.reflect: Even among the ruins, do I believe there is a way back to God?

quiz.q: Who was the Babylonian commander of the guard who burned the temple of the Lord and the palace?
quiz.explain: Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem and burned the temple, the palace and all the houses (2 Kgs 25:8–9).

events.title: By the Rivers of Babylon
events.subtitle: The day the prison door opened
story: Only a few poor people were left in the ruined land of Judah, and the king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah, grandson of Shaphan, to govern them. When the army commanders who had scattered came to him at Mizpah, Gedaliah gave them his promise: “Do not be afraid of the Babylonians. Stay in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and all will go well with you.” But in the seventh month of that year, Ishmael, a man of the royal family, came with ten men and killed Gedaliah.

The people who were left were afraid that Babylon would take revenge for this, so they all fled down to Egypt. At that time, far away in a Babylonian prison, Jehoiachin king of Judah was locked up. He had become king at eighteen, and after only three months he had been carried off to Babylon. Thirty-seven years passed for him in prison that way.

It was the last month of the year that Evil-merodach became the new king of Babylon. The new king brought Jehoiachin out of prison, treated him kindly, and gave him a seat higher than those of the other kings held captive in Babylon. Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes, and for the rest of his life he ate at the king's table. The people carried off to Babylon sang this song: by the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept as we remembered Zion.

words.text: Do not be afraid of the Babylonian officials. Live in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you.
In the year Evil-merodach became king of Babylon, he released Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison. He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat higher than the other kings who were with him.
Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes, and every day for the rest of his life he ate in the king's presence.

events.note: Clay tablets found at the site of the palace in Babylon record rations of oil given to “Ya'ukin, king of Judah” and his sons. Jehoiachin had been carried from Jerusalem to Babylon in 597 BC.
events.reflect: Even when it all seems over, can I keep holding on to God's promise?
